runs.query: employer vicariously liable for an employee who posted staff payroll data online out of a grudge

results.name: Various Claimants v WM Morrisons Supermarket Plc (Rev 1)

highlights.quote: This group action raises the question whether an employer is liable, directly or vicariously, for the criminal actions of a rogue employee in disclosing personal information of co-employees on the web, whether under the Data Protection Act 1998, an action for breach of confidence, or in an action for misuse of private information.
On 12th January 2014 a file containing personal details of 99,998 employees of the Defendant (“Morrisons”) was posted on a file sharing website.

It was not difficult to see that if a personal grudge, arising outside the work place, manifested itself in a violent action inside it, where being at work was merely the occasion for an action which might as well have happened elsewhere, it might be expected that the court would hold the employee liable on his own, and that no secondary liability would attach to the employer.

results.name: WM Morrison Supermarkets Plc v Various Claimants

highlights.quote: The central issue on this appeal is whether, on the facts, an employer is liable in damages to those of its current or former employees whose personal and confidential information has been misused by being disclosed on the web by the criminal act of another employee, who had a grudge against the employer, in breach of the Data Protection Act 1998

We consider it is clear, however, that whatever the position on the first ground of appeal, the vicarious liability of an employer for misuse of private information by an employee and for breach of confidence by an employee has not been excluded by the DPA.
Before these can be vicarious liability, all the features of the wrong which are necessary to make the employee liable have to have occurred in the course of the employment.

results.name: WM Morrison Supermarkets plc v Various Claimants

highlights.quote: First, the disclosure of the data on the Internet did not form part of Skelton’s functions or field of activities, in the sense in which those words were used by Lord Toulson: it was not an act which he was authorised to do, as Lord Nicholls put it.

Thirdly, although there was a close temporal link and an unbroken chain of causation linking the provision of the data to Skelton for the purpose of transmitting it to KPMG and his disclosing it on the Internet, a temporal or causal connection does not in itself satisfy the close connection test.
Clearly, the mere fact that Skelton’s employment gave him the opportunity to commit the wrongful act would not be sufficient to warrant the imposition of vicarious liability

The imposition of a statutory liability upon a data controller is not inconsistent with the imposition of a common law vicarious liability upon his employer, either for the breach of duties imposed by the DPA, or for breaches of duties arising under the common law or in equity.

The internal auditor carried out that task but also unlawfully copied the data and uploaded it onto a publicly accessible website, in pursuance of a vendetta against the defendant and intending thereby to cause harm to the defendant.

the direct physical interface between the police and the public, in the course of an arrest placing an innocent passer-by or bystander at risk, as falling within a now established area of general police liability for positive negligent conduct which foreseeably and directly inflicts physical injury on the public.

results.name: Curtis (A.K.A Jason) Davis v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis

The case squarely addresses whether a shape of a taxi can constitute a valid trade mark, considering inherent and acquired distinctiveness and the "shape gives substantial value" objection. The highlights directly state the very issue in question.

ewhc/ch/2016/52.rationale: This case is directly on point: it concerns whether the shape of the London taxi (the CTM and UKTM) functions as a trade mark indicating origin. The highlighted paragraphs address precisely the question of whether consumers identify the source of taxis because of their shape, and hold that the shape was not distinctive of source. It is a directly relevant authority on the shape of a taxi as a trade mark.

ewhc/ch/2015/1840.rationale: This case is directly on point: it is part of the London Taxi Corporation v Frazer-Nash litigation concerning whether the shape/appearance of London black cabs (Fairway, TX1, TX4) can be protected as registered trade marks and via passing off. The Claimant asserted Community and UK trade marks depicting the cab shapes and pleaded that the vehicles share a common design language making them instantly recognisable as London black cabs. Although this particular judgment concerns the admissibility of survey evidence, the substantive dispute is about the shape of a taxi as a trade mark, making it a directly relevant authority for a lawyer researching that question.

ewca/civ/2004/1690.rationale: The question concerns the registrability of the shape of a taxi as a trade mark. Bongrain is a leading Court of Appeal authority on the registrability and distinctive character of three-dimensional shape marks generally, but it is specifically about the shape of a cheese. The legal principles it states (that unusual or fancy shapes are not automatically distinctive, that acquired distinctiveness through use may suffice, and that the essential function of a mark is indication of origin) apply equally to any shape-of-goods application, including a taxi shape, making it substantively useful to a lawyer researching the question. However, it is not directly on-point as to the specific mark (a taxi) and so does not merit grade 3.
